proposal.name: Exponential lower bounds for deterministic strategy iteration
proposal.description:
## Motivation

A **parity game** is a finite graph game in which two players choose an infinite walk and the largest priority recurring on the walk determines the winner. Such games supply algorithmic tasks in verification. An algorithm may solve many practical instances quickly and still require many updates on a deliberately constructed family. This mission concerns the number of updates made by two specified strategy-improvement rules. It formalizes a known lower-bound result, rather than asking whether parity games themselves have polynomial-time algorithms. The source is [Friedmann's 2011 journal treatment](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0778), extending his LICS 2009 work.

## Setting

The formal model uses finite vertex sets, a total directed edge relation, an owner for each vertex, and distinct natural-number priorities. Player 0 is encoded by `false`; player 1 is encoded by `true`. A **positional strategy** chooses one legal successor at each vertex owned by that player. Its values at other vertices are ignored.

Two strategies and a starting vertex determine an eventually periodic walk. Its **valuation** has three components: the largest recurring priority, the set of more important vertices preceding the first visit to its dominating cycle vertex, and the number of steps before that visit. The cycle component is compared first. For equal cycle components, the largest priority in the symmetric difference of the two path sets decides their ordering, with an even priority favorable to player 0. A remaining length comparison favors a shorter route to an even cycle and a longer route to an odd cycle. The valuation of one player-0 strategy at a vertex is the minimum over actual legal player-1 replies.

A **local update** chooses a successor with greatest current valuation at every player-0 vertex. A **global update** chooses a strategy with greatest resulting valuations among strategies allowed by the current improvement arena. Every active update must contain a strict improvement. A complete execution starts at its stated initial strategy, performs improving updates, and stops precisely when no improving switch remains. Its cost counts updates, excluding the initial strategy.

## Formalization targets

The goal includes the two parity-game rules and their payoff-game counterparts. For each rule the required family has a constant $C>0$, independent of its parameter $n$, such that

$$|E_n|\le Cn,\qquad T_n\ge 2^n\quad(n>0).$$

For parity games the priorities are also bounded by $Cn$. An instance must admit a complete execution, and every complete execution respecting the stated rule must meet the lower bound. This explicitly prevents a universal claim about executions from becoming true merely because no execution exists. The two rules may use different hard families.

Supporting targets cover simultaneous optimal counterstrategies, strict improvement, extraction of both winning regions at termination, the local-rule lower bound, binary-outdegree refinements, discounted payoff equations, comparison preservation under reduction, and absorption values for stopping stochastic games. Discounted and stochastic lower bounds are separate supporting results within this paper's mission. Mean-payoff policy iteration is represented through the paper's specified reduction to discounted games.

## Significance

The requested artifact is a reusable formal interface for constructing and analyzing long algorithm executions. It exposes the improvement arena, counterstrategy minimization, strictness of updates, termination condition, and cost model. Subsequent constructions can use those interfaces without encoding their own meaning of an iteration.

The mathematical lower bounds are already published. The open items here are proof obligations for these explicit Lean models. Successful elaboration checks the declarations' types; it does not prove the lower bounds or establish that the definitions match the paper. The goal needs actual witness games and initial strategies, together with execution analysis. Neither a structure field assuming a long run nor a hypothesis asserting the desired growth can discharge it.

## Difficulty

A large number of possible strategies does not establish that an algorithm visits them. The lower-bound obligation concerns the updates actually permitted by the selected rule and their stopping condition. Global updates additionally compare the resulting valuations of complete successor strategies, so a definition based only on locally greatest current values would describe a different rule. Equal-valued choices also need care: the target ranges over every complete execution admitted by its relation.

Counterstrategy minima are constrained by legal replies. Their existence, the validity of the ultimately periodic valuation, and the connection between non-improvability and winning regions remain mathematical proof obligations. The payoff models add matrix nonsingularity and the interpretation of rational equation solutions.

## Formalization scope

Game size means edge count. It does not mean binary coefficient encoding length. The parity targets retain the linear-edge refinement in the source's Section 7 and the corresponding global-rule refinement in Section 8; the basic quadratic-edge drawings alone are insufficient for that stated size bound. The goal states existence of hard families, leaving their construction to the proof. It does not transcribe the source's specific vertex-label tables as unchecked constants.

Discounted games use rational rewards and a rational discount strictly between zero and one. For fixed strategies, values are defined by the exact rational inverse of $I-\beta P$. The associated milestone requires the unique discounted Bellman solution. The mean-payoff target explicitly uses rewards $(-|V|)^{\Omega(v)}$ and the specified near-one discount. It does not replace the source algorithm with an update based only on raw mean rewards, which the source warns can stall.

Stopping stochastic games have separate Max, Min and random vertices, two distinct terminals, nonnegative rational transition probabilities with row sum one, and a positive-probability route to a terminal from each state under every legal strategy pair. Values solve the finite absorption equations. The model allows arbitrary random probabilities and outdegrees, as in the source's treatment. The matrix and counterstrategy definitions are shared infrastructure; none contains an unproved lower-bound assertion.

## Selected references

- Oliver Friedmann, *An Exponential Lower Bound for the Latest Deterministic Strategy Iteration Algorithms*, Logical Methods in Computer Science, 2011. [Author PDF](https://oliverfriedmann.com/downloads/papers/strategy_improvement_lower_bound_journal.pdf), [arXiv version](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0778).
- Oliver Friedmann, *An Exponential Lower Bound for the Parity Game Strategy Improvement Algorithm as We Know it*, LICS, 2009. [Author PDF](https://oliverfriedmann.com/downloads/papers/strategy_improvement_lower_bound.pdf).

import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Prod
import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Lattice.Fold
import Mathlib.Order.ConditionallyCompleteLattice.Basic
import Mathlib.Logic.Function.Iterate

set_option autoImplicit false

/-!
Finite parity games and the Vöge–Jurdziński valuation, as in Friedmann,
LMCS 2011, §§2–4. `false` denotes player 0. Functions representing strategies
are ignored at the other player's vertices. Definitions contain no open proofs.
-/
namespace FriedmannParity

structure Game (V : Type) where
  owner : V → Bool
  priority : V → ℕ
  edge : V → V → Prop

variable {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

def WellFormed (G : Game V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, ∃ w, G.edge v w) ∧ Function.Injective G.priority

def Legal (G : Game V) (player : Bool) (σ : V → V) : Prop :=
  ∀ v, G.owner v = player → G.edge v (σ v)

def play (G : Game V) (σ τ : V → V) (v : V) : ℕ → V :=
  fun t => (fun w => if G.owner w = false then σ w else τ w)^[t] v

noncomputable def recurring (π : ℕ → V) : Finset V := by
  classical
  exact Finset.univ.filter (fun v => ∀ t, ∃ k, t ≤ k ∧ π k = v)

structure Valuation (V : Type) where
  cyclePriority : ℕ
  path : Finset V
  length : ℕ
  deriving DecidableEq

/- The finite orbit always has a recurring vertex. Thus `sup` and the least index have
their ordinary intended meanings on finite games; the valuation milestone makes
this obligation explicit. Empty V has no starting vertex. -/
noncomputable def playValue (G : Game V) (σ τ : V → V) (v : V) : Valuation V := by
  classical
  let π := play G σ τ v
  let p := (recurring π).sup G.priority
  let w := if h : ∃ w, w ∈ recurring π ∧ G.priority w = p
    then Classical.choose h else v
  let k := if h : ∃ k : ℕ, π k = w then Nat.find h else 0
  exact ⟨p, ((Finset.range k).image π).filter (fun w => p < G.priority w), k⟩

def reward (p : ℕ) : ℤ := if p % 2 = 0 then (p : ℤ) else -(p : ℤ)

def SetLT (G : Game V) (A B : Finset V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w, w ∈ (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A) ∧
    (∀ u ∈ (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A), G.priority u ≤ G.priority w) ∧
    ((G.priority w % 2 = 0 ∧ w ∈ B) ∨ (G.priority w % 2 = 1 ∧ w ∈ A))

def ValueLT (G : Game V) (a b : Valuation V) : Prop :=
  reward a.cyclePriority < reward b.cyclePriority ∨
  (a.cyclePriority = b.cyclePriority ∧ SetLT G a.path b.path) ∨
  (a.cyclePriority = b.cyclePriority ∧ a.path = b.path ∧
    ((a.cyclePriority % 2 = 1 ∧ a.length < b.length) ∨
      (a.cyclePriority % 2 = 0 ∧ b.length < a.length)))

def ValueLE (G : Game V) (a b : Valuation V) : Prop := a = b ∨ ValueLT G a b

def IsMinimum (G : Game V) (σ : V → V) (v : V) (a : Valuation V) : Prop :=
  (∃ τ, Legal G true τ ∧ playValue G σ τ v = a) ∧
  ∀ τ, Legal G true τ → ValueLE G a (playValue G σ τ v)

/- A constrained minimum of actual legal counterstrategy valuations, never an
arbitrary valuation parameter. The fallback is irrelevant once existence is
proved for the finite, total, injective-priority model. -/
noncomputable def value (G : Game V) (σ : V → V) (v : V) : Valuation V :=
  by
    classical
    exact if h : ∃ a, IsMinimum G σ v a then Classical.choose h else ⟨0, ∅, 0⟩

def OptimalCounterstrategy (G : Game V) (σ τ : V → V) : Prop :=
  Legal G true τ ∧ ∀ v τ', Legal G true τ' →
    ValueLE G (playValue G σ τ v) (playValue G σ τ' v)

def Improving (G : Game V) (σ : V → V) (v w : V) : Prop :=
  G.owner v = false ∧ G.edge v w ∧
    ValueLT G (value G σ (σ v)) (value G σ w)

def Improvable (G : Game V) (σ : V → V) : Prop := ∃ v w, Improving G σ v w

def Allowed (G : Game V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  Legal G false σ' ∧ ∀ v, G.owner v = false →
    ValueLE G (value G σ (σ v)) (value G σ (σ' v))

def Improvement (G : Game V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  Allowed G σ σ' ∧
    (Improvable G σ → ∃ v, G.owner v = false ∧
      ValueLT G (value G σ (σ v)) (value G σ (σ' v)))

def LocalStep (G : Game V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  Improvement G σ σ' ∧ ∀ v w, G.owner v = false → G.edge v w →
    ValueLE G (value G σ w) (value G σ (σ' v))

def GlobalStep (G : Game V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  Improvement G σ σ' ∧ ∀ ρ, Allowed G σ ρ → ∀ v,
    ValueLE G (value G ρ v) (value G σ' v)

def CompleteRun (G : Game V) (step : (V → V) → (V → V) → Prop)
    (ι : V → V) (T : ℕ) (run : ℕ → (V → V)) : Prop :=
  run 0 = ι ∧ (∀ t, t ≤ T → Legal G false (run t)) ∧
    (∀ t, t < T → Improvable G (run t) ∧ step (run t) (run (t + 1))) ∧
    ¬ Improvable G (run T)

noncomputable def edgeCount (G : Game V) : ℕ := by
  classical
  exact (Finset.univ.filter (fun e : V × V => G.edge e.1 e.2)).card

def HardInstance (G : Game V) (ι : V → V)
    (step : (V → V) → (V → V) → Prop) (iterations : ℕ) : Prop :=
  WellFormed G ∧ Legal G false ι ∧
    (∃ T run, CompleteRun G step ι T run) ∧
    ∀ T run, CompleteRun G step ι T run → iterations ≤ T

/- Both families, including their size bound, are conclusions to be proved.
No field or hypothesis supplies a long execution. The constant is uniform in n.
Size is edges, as in the source, rather than vertices or numeric bit length. -/
def ExponentialLocal : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∃ G : Game (Fin N), ∃ ι : Fin N → Fin N,
      edgeCount G ≤ C * n ∧
      (∀ v, G.priority v ≤ C * n) ∧ HardInstance G ι (LocalStep G) (2 ^ n)

def ExponentialGlobal : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∃ G : Game (Fin N), ∃ ι : Fin N → Fin N,
      edgeCount G ≤ C * n ∧
      (∀ v, G.priority v ≤ C * n) ∧ HardInstance G ι (GlobalStep G) (2 ^ n)

def Binary (G : Game V) : Prop :=
  ∀ v, ∃ a b, ∀ w, G.edge v w → w = a ∨ w = b

def ExponentialBinary : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ global : Bool, ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∃ G : Game (Fin N), ∃ ι : Fin N → Fin N,
      Binary G ∧ edgeCount G ≤ C * n ∧
      (∀ v, G.priority v ≤ C * n) ∧
      HardInstance G ι (if global then GlobalStep G else LocalStep G) (2 ^ n)

def Wins (G : Game V) (player : Bool) (σ : V → V) (v : V) : Prop :=
  Legal G player σ ∧ ∀ τ, Legal G (!player) τ →
    (if player = false then (playValue G σ τ v).cyclePriority % 2 = 0
      else (playValue G τ σ v).cyclePriority % 2 = 1)

def WinningRegion (G : Game V) (player : Bool) : Set V :=
  {v | ∃ σ, Wins G player σ v}

def IsSinkGame (G : Game V) (ι : V → V) (sink : V) : Prop :=
  WellFormed G ∧ Legal G false ι ∧
    G.edge sink sink ∧ G.priority sink = 1 ∧
    (∀ v, v ≠ sink → 1 < G.priority v) ∧
    (∀ v, Relation.ReflTransGen G.edge v sink) ∧
    ∀ σ, Legal G false σ →
      (∀ v, ValueLE G (value G ι v) (value G σ v)) →
      ∀ v, (value G σ v).cyclePriority = 1

end FriedmannParity
items.natural_language_statement: Finite positional parity games, ultimately periodic plays, three-component valuations, minima over legal counterstrategies, local and global improvement, completed executions, and constrained lower-bound propositions. No witness family or long execution is assumed.
items.readback: For an arbitrary type $V$, a game is the record of a Boolean owner, a natural priority, and an edge relation; a valuation is the record of a natural cycle priority, a finite vertex set, and a natural length. A parity game on a finite set $V$ equipped with decidable equality consists of an owner $o:V\to\{0,1\}$, a priority $d:V\to\mathbb N$, and an edge relation $E\subseteq V\times V$; owner $0$ means the Boolean false and owner $1$ means true. A strategy is a total function $V\to V$ and is legal for player $i$ exactly when $E(v,\sigma(v))$ holds for every $v$ with $o(v)=i$; its values at the other player's vertices are unrestricted. The predicate called well formed means exactly that every vertex has an outgoing edge and that the priority function is injective. For any total functions $\sigma,\tau:V\to V$ and start $v\in V$, put $f(u)=\sigma(u)$ if $o(u)=0$ and $f(u)=\tau(u)$ otherwise, and $\pi_t=f^t(v)$ for $t\in\mathbb N$, including $\pi_0=v$. Let $R=\{u\in V:\forall t\in\mathbb N\ \exists k\in\mathbb N,\ k\ge t\ \text{and}\ \pi_k=u\}$ and let $p=\max\{d(u):u\in R\}$, with maximum $0$ when $R$ is empty. If a vertex of $R$ has priority $p$, classically choose one such vertex $z$; otherwise set $z=v$. Let $k$ be the least natural index for which $\pi_k=z$ if such an index exists, and $0$ otherwise, and let $A=\{\pi_j:0\le j<k,\ p<d(\pi_j)\}$. Write $P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)=(p,A,k)$; $A$ is a set, so repetitions are discarded. Selection among multiple recurring vertices of priority $p$ is by classical choice. This construction is defined without a legality or well-formedness assumption; for an actual start in a finite $V$, some recurring vertex exists and the maximum recurring priority is attained, whereas an empty $V$ has no start. A valuation is any triple $(p,A,k)$ with $p,k\in\mathbb N$ and $A\subseteq V$. Define $r(p)=p$ for even $p$ and $r(p)=-p$ for odd $p$, as an integer. For finite sets $A,B$, write $A\triangleleft B$ if there exists $w$ in their symmetric difference such that $d(u)\le d(w)$ for every $u$ in that difference, and either $d(w)$ is even and $w\in B$, or $d(w)$ is odd and $w\in A$; an empty symmetric difference cannot satisfy this relation, and a maximum-priority witness is not required to be unique. For $a=(p,A,k)$ and $b=(q,B,\ell)$, define $a\prec b$ to mean $r(p)<r(q)$, or $p=q$ and $A\triangleleft B$, or $p=q$, $A=B$, and either $p$ is odd with $k<\ell$, or $p$ is even with $\ell<k$; define $a\preceq b$ to mean $a=b$ or $a\prec b$. The predicate that a valuation is a minimum at $\sigma,v$ says it is attained by a legal player-$1$ strategy and is $\preceq$ every valuation obtained from any legal player-$1$ strategy at that same $\sigma,v$. For each $\sigma$ and $v$, $Q_\sigma(v)$ is a classically chosen valuation $a$ such that some legal player-$1$ strategy $\tau$ has $P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)=a$ and $a\preceq P_{\sigma,\tau'}(v)$ for every legal player-$1$ strategy $\tau'$, if such an attained least valuation exists; if none exists, $Q_\sigma(v)=(0,\varnothing,0)$. This minimization is defined separately at each start and does not assume that $\sigma$ is legal. An optimal counterstrategy against $\sigma$ is one legal player-$1$ function $\tau$ satisfying $P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)\preceq P_{\sigma,\tau'}(v)$ simultaneously for every vertex $v$ and every legal player-$1$ function $\tau'$. An improving edge for $\sigma$ is a pair $(v,w)$ with $o(v)=0$, $E(v,w)$, and $Q_\sigma(\sigma(v))\prec Q_\sigma(w)$; $\sigma$ is improvable if at least one such pair exists. An update $\sigma\mapsto\sigma'$ is allowed if $\sigma'$ is legal for player $0$ and $Q_\sigma(\sigma(v))\preceq Q_\sigma(\sigma'(v))$ at every player-$0$ vertex. An improvement is an allowed update which, whenever $\sigma$ is improvable, also satisfies $Q_\sigma(\sigma(v))\prec Q_\sigma(\sigma'(v))$ at at least one player-$0$ vertex; if $\sigma$ is not improvable, this last implication imposes no extra requirement. A local step is an improvement such that $Q_\sigma(w)\preceq Q_\sigma(\sigma'(v))$ for every player-$0$ vertex $v$ and every edge $E(v,w)$. A global step is an improvement such that $Q_\rho(v)\preceq Q_{\sigma'}(v)$ for every total strategy $\rho$ allowed from $\sigma$ and every $v\in V$, with each $Q_\rho$ computed using $\rho$ as the player-$0$ strategy. For any chosen binary step relation on strategies, a complete run is a natural number $T$ and an infinite sequence $(\sigma_t)_{t\in\mathbb N}$ of total functions with $\sigma_0=\iota$, every $\sigma_t$ legal for player $0$ for $t\le T$, and, for every $t<T$, $\sigma_t$ improvable and a step from $\sigma_t$ to $\sigma_{t+1}$, while $\sigma_T$ is not improvable; values of the sequence after $T$ are unrestricted, and $T=0$ is permitted. A hard instance for a natural lower bound $L$ requires that every vertex have an outgoing edge, that $d$ be injective, that $\iota$ be legal for player $0$, that at least one such complete run exist, and that every such complete run have $L\le T$. The edge count is the cardinality of $\{(v,w)\in V\times V:E(v,w)\}$. The local exponential proposition asserts that there is a natural constant $C>0$ such that for every natural $n>0$ there exist a natural $N$, a parity game on $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$, and an initial total strategy $\iota$, with at most $Cn$ ordered edges and $d(v)\le Cn$ for every vertex, forming a hard instance with $L=2^n$ for local steps. The global exponential proposition makes the same assertion with global steps. The constant is uniform in $n$, the witnesses may depend on $n$, no condition is requested for $n=0$, and $N$ is quantified over all natural numbers, including $0$, subject to the stated requirements. The binary-arena predicate means that for every vertex $v$ there exist vertices $a,b$ such that every $w$ with $E(v,w)$ satisfies $w=a$ or $w=b$. The witnesses $a,b$ may depend on $v$, may coincide, and need not themselves be successors of $v$; thus at most two successors are allowed, rather than exactly two. This predicate is vacuous for an empty vertex set. The binary exponential proposition asserts that there is a natural constant $C>0$ such that, for every Boolean rule choice and every natural $n>0$, there exist a natural $N$, a binary parity game on $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$, and an initial total function $\iota$, with at most $Cn$ ordered edges and priority at most $Cn$ at every vertex, forming a hard instance of bound $2^n$ for global steps if the Boolean is true and local steps if it is false. The same $C$ works for both choices and all positive $n$, whereas $N,G,\iota$ may depend on both choices and $n$. A total function $\sigma$ wins for player $0$ at $v$ precisely when it is legal for player $0$ and, for every legal player-$1$ function $\tau$, the first coordinate of $P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)$ is even; it wins for player $1$ at $v$ precisely when it is legal for player $1$ and, for every legal player-$0$ function $\tau$, the first coordinate of $P_{\tau,\sigma}(v)$ is odd. The winning region of a player is the set of vertices at which there exists such a winning total function, with the existential function allowed to depend on the vertex. Finally, the sink-game predicate for an arena $G$, initial function $\iota$, and specified vertex $s$ requires well-formedness, player-$0$ legality of $\iota$, an edge $E(s,s)$, $d(s)=1$, $d(v)>1$ for every $v\ne s$, a finite edge path from every $v$ to $s$ allowing a path of length zero, and the following universal implication: for every player-$0$ legal $\sigma$, if $Q_\iota(v)\preceq Q_\sigma(v)$ at every vertex, then the first coordinate of $Q_\sigma(v)$ is $1$ at every vertex. The definition does not assign an owner to the distinguished sink. All universal vertex conditions include the empty-vertex-set case where their types permit it, and no separate nonemptiness assumption is made.

items.definition_title: Rational payoff and stopping stochastic game models
items.definition:
import Definitions.Def_friedmann_parity
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.NonsingularInverse

set_option autoImplicit false

open Matrix

namespace FriedmannScalar

open scoped BigOperators

variable {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/- A common interface for the actual payoff models below. Every instance in a
mission target is constructed from a concrete game, not supplied as a hypothesis.
-/
structure Model (V : Type) where
  maxNode : V → Prop
  action : V → V → Prop
  maxLegal : (V → V) → Prop
  minLegal : (V → V) → Prop
  payoff : (V → V) → (V → V) → V → ℚ

noncomputable def value (M : Model V) (σ : V → V) (v : V) : ℚ := by
  classical
  exact if h : ∃ a : ℚ,
      (∃ τ, M.minLegal τ ∧ M.payoff σ τ v = a) ∧
        ∀ τ, M.minLegal τ → a ≤ M.payoff σ τ v
    then Classical.choose h else 0

def Improving (M : Model V) (σ : V → V) (v w : V) : Prop :=
  M.maxNode v ∧ M.action v w ∧ value M σ (σ v) < value M σ w

def Improvable (M : Model V) (σ : V → V) : Prop := ∃ v w, Improving M σ v w

def Allowed (M : Model V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  M.maxLegal σ' ∧ ∀ v, M.maxNode v → value M σ (σ v) ≤ value M σ (σ' v)

def Improvement (M : Model V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  Allowed M σ σ' ∧ (Improvable M σ →
    ∃ v, M.maxNode v ∧ value M σ (σ v) < value M σ (σ' v))

def LocalStep (M : Model V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  Improvement M σ σ' ∧ ∀ v w, M.maxNode v → M.action v w →
    value M σ w ≤ value M σ (σ' v)

def GlobalStep (M : Model V) (σ σ' : V → V) : Prop :=
  Improvement M σ σ' ∧ ∀ ρ, Allowed M σ ρ → ∀ v, value M ρ v ≤ value M σ' v

def CompleteRun (M : Model V) (step : (V → V) → (V → V) → Prop)
    (ι : V → V) (T : ℕ) (run : ℕ → (V → V)) : Prop :=
  run 0 = ι ∧ (∀ t, t ≤ T → M.maxLegal (run t)) ∧
    (∀ t, t < T → Improvable M (run t) ∧ step (run t) (run (t + 1))) ∧
    ¬ Improvable M (run T)

def HardInstance (M : Model V) (ι : V → V)
    (step : (V → V) → (V → V) → Prop) (iterations : ℕ) : Prop :=
  M.maxLegal ι ∧ (∃ T run, CompleteRun M step ι T run) ∧
    ∀ T run, CompleteRun M step ι T run → iterations ≤ T

def rule (M : Model V) (global : Bool) : (V → V) → (V → V) → Prop :=
  if global then GlobalStep M else LocalStep M

end FriedmannScalar

namespace FriedmannDiscounted

open scoped BigOperators

structure Game (V : Type) where
  arena : FriedmannParity.Game V
  reward : V → ℚ
  discount : ℚ

variable {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

def WellFormed (G : Game V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, ∃ w, G.arena.edge v w) ∧ 0 < G.discount ∧ G.discount < 1

noncomputable def transition (G : Game V) (σ τ : V → V) : Matrix V V ℚ := by
  classical
  exact fun v w => if (if G.arena.owner v = false then σ v else τ v) = w then 1 else 0

/- Exact rational solution of x = r + βPx. For 0 < β < 1 the matrix is
nonsingular, and this is the infinite discounted sum of the actual play. -/
noncomputable def playValue (G : Game V) (σ τ : V → V) : V → ℚ :=
  (1 - G.discount • transition G σ τ)⁻¹ *ᵥ G.reward

noncomputable def model (G : Game V) : FriedmannScalar.Model V where
  maxNode v := G.arena.owner v = false
  action := G.arena.edge
  maxLegal := FriedmannParity.Legal G.arena false
  minLegal := FriedmannParity.Legal G.arena true
  payoff := playValue G

noncomputable def induced (G : FriedmannParity.Game V) : Game V := by
  classical
  let r : V → ℚ := fun v => (-(Fintype.card V : ℚ)) ^ G.priority v
  let maxReward : ℕ := Finset.univ.sup (fun v => (Fintype.card V) ^ G.priority v)
  exact ⟨G, r, 1 - 1 / (4 * (Fintype.card V : ℚ) ^ 3 * (maxReward : ℚ))⟩

def Exponential : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ global : Bool, ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∃ G : Game (Fin N), ∃ ι : Fin N → Fin N,
      WellFormed G ∧ FriedmannParity.edgeCount G.arena ≤ C * n ∧

namespace FriedmannStochastic

open scoped BigOperators

/- Roles 0 and 1 are Max and Min; role 2 is a random vertex. The two terminals
are excluded from these decision sets by explicit tests in every definition. -/
structure Game (V : Type) where
  role : V → Fin 3
  edge : V → V → Prop
  probability : V → V → ℚ
  win : V
  lose : V

variable {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

def Decision (G : Game V) (p : Fin 3) (v : V) : Prop :=
  v ≠ G.win ∧ v ≠ G.lose ∧ G.role v = p

def Legal (G : Game V) (p : Fin 3) (σ : V → V) : Prop :=
  ∀ v, Decision G p v → G.edge v (σ v)

noncomputable def transition (G : Game V) (σ τ : V → V) : Matrix V V ℚ := by
  classical
  exact fun v w => if v = G.win ∨ v = G.lose then 0
    else if G.role v = 0 then (if σ v = w then 1 else 0)
    else if G.role v = 1 then (if τ v = w then 1 else 0)
    else G.probability v w

def WellFormed (G : Game V) : Prop :=
  G.win ≠ G.lose ∧
  (∀ v, v ≠ G.win → v ≠ G.lose → ∃ w, G.edge v w) ∧
  (∀ w, ¬ G.edge G.win w ∧ ¬ G.edge G.lose w) ∧
  (∀ v w, Decision G 2 v → 0 ≤ G.probability v w ∧
    (¬ G.edge v w → G.probability v w = 0)) ∧
  (∀ v, Decision G 2 v → ∑ w, G.probability v w = 1) ∧
  ∀ σ τ, Legal G 0 σ → Legal G 1 τ → ∀ v,
    Relation.ReflTransGen (fun a b => 0 < transition G σ τ a b) v G.win ∨
    Relation.ReflTransGen (fun a b => 0 < transition G σ τ a b) v G.lose

/- Absorption probabilities, obtained from the finite transient transition
matrix. Almost-sure halting in WellFormed makes I-P nonsingular. -/
noncomputable def playValue (G : Game V) (σ τ : V → V) : V → ℚ := by
  classical
  exact (1 - transition G σ τ)⁻¹ *ᵥ (fun v => if v = G.win then 1 else 0)

noncomputable def model (G : Game V) : FriedmannScalar.Model V where
  maxNode := Decision G 0
  action := G.edge
  maxLegal := Legal G 0
  minLegal := Legal G 1
  payoff := playValue G

noncomputable def edgeCount (G : Game V) : ℕ := by
  classical
  exact (Finset.univ.filter (fun e : V × V => G.edge e.1 e.2)).card

def Exponential : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ global : Bool, ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∃ G : Game (Fin N), ∃ ι : Fin N → Fin N,
      WellFormed G ∧ edgeCount G ≤ C * n ∧
      FriedmannScalar.HardInstance (model G) ι
        (FriedmannScalar.rule (model G) global) (2 ^ n)

end FriedmannStochastic

items.readback: For every finite vertex set $V$ equipped with decidable equality, every parity game $G$ on $V$ such that each vertex has an outgoing edge and its natural priority function is injective, and every total function $\sigma:V\to V$ legal for player $0$, the assertion is that there exists a single total function $\tau:V\to V$ legal for player $1$ which simultaneously minimizes the play valuation at every start: for every $v\in V$ and every legal player-$1$ function $\tau'$, $P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)\preceq P_{\sigma,\tau'}(v)$, and for every $v\in V$, $Q_\sigma(v)=P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)$. A parity game on a finite set $V$ equipped with decidable equality consists of an owner $o:V\to\{0,1\}$, a priority $d:V\to\mathbb N$, and an edge relation $E\subseteq V\times V$; owner $0$ means the Boolean false and owner $1$ means true. A strategy is a total function $V\to V$ and is legal for player $i$ exactly when $E(v,\sigma(v))$ holds for every $v$ with $o(v)=i$; its values at the other player's vertices are unrestricted. For any total functions $\sigma,\tau:V\to V$ and start $v\in V$, put $f(u)=\sigma(u)$ if $o(u)=0$ and $f(u)=\tau(u)$ otherwise, and $\pi_t=f^t(v)$ for $t\in\mathbb N$, including $\pi_0=v$. Let $R=\{u\in V:\forall t\in\mathbb N\ \exists k\in\mathbb N,\ k\ge t\ \text{and}\ \pi_k=u\}$ and let $p=\max\{d(u):u\in R\}$, with maximum $0$ when $R$ is empty. If a vertex of $R$ has priority $p$, classically choose one such vertex $z$; otherwise set $z=v$. Let $k$ be the least natural index for which $\pi_k=z$ if such an index exists, and $0$ otherwise, and let $A=\{\pi_j:0\le j<k,\ p<d(\pi_j)\}$. Write $P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)=(p,A,k)$; $A$ is a set, so repetitions are discarded. Selection among multiple recurring vertices of priority $p$ is by classical choice. This construction is defined without a legality or well-formedness assumption; for an actual start in a finite $V$, some recurring vertex exists and the maximum recurring priority is attained, whereas an empty $V$ has no start. A valuation is any triple $(p,A,k)$ with $p,k\in\mathbb N$ and $A\subseteq V$. Define $r(p)=p$ for even $p$ and $r(p)=-p$ for odd $p$, as an integer. For finite sets $A,B$, write $A\triangleleft B$ if there exists $w$ in their symmetric difference such that $d(u)\le d(w)$ for every $u$ in that difference, and either $d(w)$ is even and $w\in B$, or $d(w)$ is odd and $w\in A$; an empty symmetric difference cannot satisfy this relation, and a maximum-priority witness is not required to be unique. This minimization is defined separately at each start and does not assume that $\sigma$ is legal. The witness $\tau$ is shared by all starting vertices. No nonemptiness hypothesis on $V$ is imposed; for empty $V$ all start-indexed conclusions are vacuous.

items.natural_language_statement: For a non-improvable legal strategy, even and odd dominating cycle priorities identify exactly the two positional winning regions. The current player-0 strategy wins on its region; every optimal player-1 counterstrategy wins on the other region; and the current strategy has pointwise greatest valuation.

For any chosen binary step relation on strategies, a complete run is a natural number $T$ and an infinite sequence $(\sigma_t)_{t\in\mathbb N}$ of total functions with $\sigma_0=\iota$, every $\sigma_t$ legal for player $0$ for $t\le T$, and, for every $t<T$, $\sigma_t$ improvable and a step from $\sigma_t$ to $\sigma_{t+1}$, while $\sigma_T$ is not improvable; values of the sequence after $T$ are unrestricted, and $T=0$ is permitted. A hard instance for a natural lower bound $L$ requires that every vertex have an outgoing edge, that $d$ be injective, that $\iota$ be legal for player $0$, that at least one such complete run exist, and that every such complete run have $L\le T$. The constant is uniform in both $g$ and all positive $n$, and the witnesses may depend on $g,n$. No assertion is made for $n=0$. The quantifier over $N$ includes $0$ subject to all the requirements; binary branching by itself is vacuous on an empty set, while the existence and lower-bound requirements are also part of this assertion.

items.theorem_title: Preservation of valuation comparisons under reduction
items.natural_language_statement: In a finite injective-priority 1-sink game, take any legal strategy whose valuations are pointwise no worse than the initial strategy. Strict comparisons between the valuations of any two vertices agree exactly with strict comparisons of their values in the specified induced discounted game.

milestones.milestone_description: For every finite total parity game with distinct priorities and every legal positional player-0 strategy, one legal positional player-1 reply simultaneously minimizes the play valuation at all starting vertices and realizes the defined valuation.
A legal strategy update in the improvement arena, containing a strict switch whenever the original strategy is improvable, weakly raises every vertex valuation and strictly raises at least one.

For a non-improvable legal strategy, even and odd dominating cycle priorities identify exactly the two positional winning regions. The current player-0 strategy wins on its region; every optimal player-1 counterstrategy wins on the other region; and the current strategy has pointwise greatest valuation.

milestones.milestone_title: Sections 6 and 7 — linear-size local lower bound
milestones.milestone_description: There is a uniform linear-size family of finite total parity games with distinct, linearly bounded priorities and legal initial strategies such that complete local-update executions exist and every such execution performs at least $2^n$ improving updates.

For any finite total rational-reward game, any rational discount strictly between zero and one, and any pair of successor functions, the matrix-defined payoff vector satisfies the fixed-strategy discounted Bellman equations, and every rational solution equals that vector. Legality of the functions is unnecessary for this equation-level statement.

For every well-formed stopping stochastic game and legal strategy pair, $I-P$ is nonsingular. Its absorption solution is one at the winning terminal, zero at the losing terminal, lies in $[0,1]$ everywhere, and satisfies the transition equations at every nonterminal state.

Both local and global improvement require at least $2^n$ updates on uniform linear-edge families of discounted games. The same lower bound holds for mean-payoff inputs when the algorithm runs through the explicitly defined standard discounted reduction. Every hard instance admits a complete execution.
Both local and global strategy improvement have uniform linear-edge families of stopping stochastic games on which complete executions exist and every complete execution makes at least $2^n$ updates.

For each of the local and global rules, uniform linear-edge hard families with linearly bounded priorities can be chosen with at most two distinct outgoing neighbors per vertex. Complete executions exist and every such execution takes at least $2^n$ updates.
